Does a rocket require less acceleration as it gets higher up into the atmosphere?

Short answer is yes, but its a bit more complicated. I don't know the specifics, but the thing about rocket science is you are dealing with an object who's mass is not constant. As the rocket ascends, there is less friction and less gravity to overcome, but the amount of mass in the object is also decreasing as its being thrown out of the engine.

For a way to convince yourself, take a look at a saturn V rocket. The first stage has 5 very large engines. The successive stages have smaller and smaller ones, until you get to the OMS which is just tiny nozzles that expend a small amount of propellant but give a huge amount of maneuverability.

As for the yo-yo despin, they are just ejecting a weight on a string that absorbs the energy of the spin and is disconnected at the proper time.

Severa things are going on, one, if you don't have a thrust to weight ratio (TWR) of higher than 1 a rocket isn't moving off the pad, and in an atmosphere you can expect to lose control of the direction the rocket is pointed below 1.15. In suborbital flight you can have much lower thrust to weight ratios (there is a limit that you have to reach 7200 m/s in order to stay in space, some minimum TWR is needed to achieve that before reentering the atmosphere), and for orbital maneuvers extremely low thrust engines are used for probes and have been proposed for a mars mission.

Secondly the rocket loses weight as it gains speed, which means you need less thrust in order to maintain the same ratio.

The gravity in low earth orbit is about 12% less powerful than on the ground, its not a major factor.

As atmosphere decreases you need less thrust to overcome friction, however your thrust is also more effective, check out the oberth effect.

At high altitude one pound of fuel will be more effective than at low altitude, but as you leave the gravity well it will become less effective. So you could burn it more slowly, but you shouldn't.

It depends what the rocket is trying to do. If you're trying to send a probe out past pluto, you shouldn't start to decelerate / turn down the throttle. If you're trying to reach a low earth orbit, eventually you're going to decrease the throttle as you get closer and closer to your desired orbit.

Literal crazy cat people.

The scary part is that it probably goes further than this. T. gondii has been shown to alter the mental processes of mice: the infected mice become less averse to cats (i.e. they like cats more; sound familiar?), and we simply don't know what effects it has on infected human minds as little research has been done. From what has:

Animal studies have shown that mice infected with T. gondii have motor performance worse than non-infected mice. In a human study with volunteer blood donors, reaction times and the amount of time the subject remained focused for were worse for the infected group than for the control group. . . A few observational studies on human subjects have also found the risk of traffic accidents to be significantly greater in infected persons than non-infected controls.

In other words, tens of millions of people are currently walking around infected with a possibly mind-altering parasite.
